Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

limn 0.0.0.9000

  • limn is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or (at your option) any later version: GPL (>= 2).
  • A new scoring rule, "wis", in ilm_scores() and ilm_cv(): the weighted interval score of Bracher et al. (2021, section 2.2). It weighs the median’s absolute error and the interval scores of central intervals at levels 1 - alpha, and needs only the prediction’s quantiles. The default alpha is theirs, the median and 11 intervals (23 quantiles), as forecast hubs report them; give alpha = for other levels. The tests reproduce the paper’s worked example with the values of its correction (Bracher et al. 2022).
  • A prediction knows its time and series columns without a correlation over time (ilm_predict(), Time and series columns):
    • rows from ilm_future() say which they are, so a model with time only in its formula, a trend or a random slope, gets the trend check, and ilm_scores(history = ) works for it;
    • time and group in ilm_predict() and ilm_forecast() now name columns of newdata, for rows made otherwise or changed by merge() or subset(). They used to take the times and groups themselves, for a correlation over time built from vectors; such a model now takes them as columns, which follow the rows through set and scenarios;
    • a correlation over time built by name keeps its own columns. Naming a different one is an error, and so are rows from ilm_future() built around a different time or series column, which leave the model’s own missing.
  • ilm_forecast() takes time and group as arguments of its own. Passed on through ..., group = was taken as groups =.
  • ilm_predict(), and everything built on it, works for a fit with a smooth that illume can predict from. It stopped with “internal: no ‘beta’ draw”, since illume’s design leaves a smooth’s unpenalised column unnamed. A factor smooth, s(t, id, bs = "fs"), and t2() still stop, inside illume.
  • The trend check also covers a random slope in time, which gives each unit a trend of its own, and rows past the data that did not come from ilm_future(). Grouping by time, as in (1 | week), is not a trend.
  • The trend check also covers a smooth of time. Many smooths continue past the data as a straight line (Clark and Wells 2023, section 1), and illume’s default smooth does. A periodic smooth, s(t, bs = "cc") or "cp", is not a trend.
  • The trend check’s advice offers both choices in place of the trend, and says that either is an assumption: ilm_ar1() or ilm_car1() when the series should return to a level, and ilm_rw1() when its level should be free to move. A model that already has an AR(1) or CAR(1) term is told to take the trend out and keep that term.
  • The help for cross-validation and model comparison cites its sources by section, equation and page, and the comparison plots say how to read them. The few-origins warning of ilm_compare() now cites Coroneo and Iacone
    1. by section (4.2 and 5) instead of by page.
  • The help for prediction and forecasting lists every element of a prediction (ilm_predict(), The prediction object), cites its sources by section, explains how to read a fan chart, and gives as.data.frame() and ilm_plot_fan() examples. Claims the sources did not support were removed: that ETS intervals leave out parameter uncertainty, and that glmmTMB and lme4 give the same point forecast.
  • The package help page (?limn) gives the workflow, explains how checks and remedies work, and has a worked example.
  • Every check’s source was read again at its page:
    • the few-groups check for means cites Kenward and Roger (1997) at pp. 983-984, not p. 983 alone;
    • the few-groups check for new units says that Maas and Hox (2005) cite Browne (1998) for restricted maximum likelihood being at least as good;
    • the typical-unit coverage the few-groups check quotes now gives binary outcomes’ 0.92 beside the 0.84 to 0.86 of the other families;
    • the trend check labels its point about intervals as limn’s own reasoning;
    • the Diebold-Mariano check pages Harvey, Leybourne and Newbold’s Table 1.
  • Checks whose remedy is a change to the model now name illume::ilm_apply_remedy() beside illume::ilm_remedies().
  • The help for scores and calibration defines every scoring rule as an R expression or formula. It cites Gneiting and Raftery (2007) by section, equation or table, and page for the log, CRPS, Brier, pinball, interval and squared-error scores, and fpp3 section 5.8 for the scaled errors; the absolute error is twice the pinball loss at 1/2. The PIT, its histogram and the calibration plot say how to read them, and ilm_pit() and ilm_plot_calibration() gain examples. The interval score is no longer called “Winkler’s”: Gneiting and Raftery trace it to Dunsmore, Winkler, and Winkler and Murphy. The calibration verdicts say which of their thresholds are limn’s own choices.
  • A test reproduces Gneiting and Raftery’s closed-form gaussian CRPS, their interval score and their quantile score.
  • A vignette, “Getting started with limn” (vignette("limn")), works through one example from fit to comparison: predictions for known and new units, a forecast, weekly totals, scores, and a calibration check whose verdict is acted on, the model refitted and checked again. The models are then compared on held-back weeks and over rolling origins. knitr and rmarkdown join Suggests, to build it.
  • A second vignette, “Predictions: which unit, and how uncertain” (vignette("predictions")), works through ilm_predict()’s choices: which unit (a fitted, new, typical or average one), the mean or a new observation, averages over a population with ilm_average(), and how much of the fit’s uncertainty to draw. It ends with the few-groups check and its remedy.
  • The few-groups check for a new unit’s observation no longer suggests refitting with reml = TRUE when the model was already fitted by restricted maximum likelihood. It still warns, and gives instead what limn’s prototype study found with REML and 8 groups: 90% intervals covered 0.892 (Poisson) and 0.903 (gaussian).
  • The help for ilm_predict()‘s uncertainty choices now says that a plug-in prediction (uncertainty = "none") still draws a new unit’s effects, and a series’ cells at times it was not fitted at. The few-groups coverage it gives for "joint" is now said to be for a new unit’s observation, against the other methods the prototype tried, with its simulation error.
  • A third vignette, “Forecasting series” (vignette("forecasting")), forecasts several series at once: the rows a forecast needs, the trend check and its remedy (a random walk in place of an autoregressive term), a covariate whose future is drawn from its own model or taken from another tool, fan charts, and totals across series and over the horizon.
  • ilm_compare(method = "dm") no longer drops to lag 0 when its long-run variance is negative.
    • It follows Diebold and Mariano’s (1995) own rule: the variance is taken as 0 and the null hypothesis rejected, so the statistic is infinite and the p-value 0. It warns, naming method = "wpe", the default, which needs no lag.
    • Results change only in that case.
  • Two generics let another package’s fits use limn.
    • ilm_predict_draws() is the step of ilm_predict() that draws the model’s parameters, and ilm_cv_refit() the step of ilm_cv() that refits the model to a fold’s training rows.
    • A package that fits illume’s models another way, by sampling a posterior say, registers methods for its own class of fit. Predictions, forecasts, scores, calibration, comparison and cross-validation then work on its fits unchanged.
    • The methods for illume’s fits are what limn did before, so every result is the same.
    • Draws in the wrong shape stop with a message saying what is wrong. Each ilm_cv(ncores = ) worker also loads the package whose methods the fit needs.
  • A prediction’s quantiles are found faster, with the same answers.
    • The mixture quantile behind calibration, the pinball and interval scores and every interval now closes its bracket by a capped Illinois secant, not by bisection alone.
    • It never takes more than two passes of the mixture’s CDF beyond the bisection’s count, and its answer agrees with the bisection’s to 1e-12.
    • On 2,000 rows by 1,000 draws, calibration took 0.62 of its earlier time on a gaussian model and 0.24 on a weibull survival model. The pinball and interval scores took 0.72.
    • Coverage, interval widths and calibration verdicts are unchanged.
  • The shared display rules write very large and very small numbers in scientific notation, as in illumex 0.0.8.9003.
    • A number is written in full up to 15 digits before the decimal point and down to 6 decimal places. Beyond either, it uses R’s form: 1.23e+300, 1.23e-30.
    • The shared file also gains a rule for a group of values written to common decimals.
    • None of limn’s usual prints changes. Only an estimate beyond those limits, such as a standard error of 1.23e-08, now reads that way, rather than as a long run of zeros.
  • Numbers are written by the family’s shared display rules, in R/shared-helpers.R, the same file byte for byte in each of the family’s packages. Each number declares what it is:
    • an estimate (a score, a difference, a standard error, a width, a test statistic) to three significant figures with its trailing zeros kept: 0.290, not 0.29;
    • a count (rows, draws, folds, clusters) whole, grouped from 1,000: “1,200 rows”;
    • a share (a coverage, an observed or predicted rate) as a percentage to three significant figures, in prints and verdicts alike: “70.4% of outcomes”, not “70%”. A coverage’s standard error is an estimate in percentage points: “(SE 1.77 percentage points)”. An interval’s level (“95%”) is a setting and is written as given;
    • a p-value by the family’s own rule.
    Rounding is half away from zero on the value’s decimal form, not on its binary one. ilm_cv()’s print now shows its mean scores to three significant figures, where it printed seven.
  • Fix: the CRPS of a continuous prediction is now exact, or integrated to a stated error, for every continuous family.
    • What was wrong. It was integrated with 16 equal panels over the range of all the draws. The panels were sized by the widest component, while the integrand’s detail is as narrow as the narrowest one.
      • Gaussian mixtures whose components differ widely in spread were off by up to 0.77% relative: sds from 0.01 to 10 across draws.
      • So were tiny-sd components with spread means, such as a forecast whose latent path varies far more than its noise: 0.1%.
      • On the positive families (lognormal, weibull, loglogistic), mixtures whose scale parameters spread up to 60-fold across draws were off by 14% to 100% relative at small and middling outcomes.
      • A loglogistic’s upper tail beyond its 1 - 1e-10 quantile was dropped: 6.6e-4 of the CRPS at s = 1.67 and 17% at s = 1.92.
      • On the shapes typical predictions have, the error was at most about 1e-11. Beta was within 1e-7.
    • Now.
      • A gaussian mixture’s CRPS is the exact closed form (Grimit et al. 2006), as scoringRules::crps_mixnorm gives it. The old quadrature is kept only for rows it has been shown to integrate to rounding.
      • Lognormal, weibull and loglogistic are integrated on log y, and beta on logit y, with panels sized by the narrowest component.
      • The upper tail comes from the survival function, never 1 - F. A loglogistic is integrated out to a stated bound on what is left.
    • Edge cases.
      • A loglogistic component with scale 2 or more makes the CRPS infinite, and it is returned as Inf, with a message.
      • A row whose integration fails is NA, named in a message, never a number.
      • A continuous family without a CRPS method is an error, not a fallback.
    • Cost, at 2,000 rows by 1,000 draws on one core: 1.19 times before for a gaussian prediction, 1.68 times for a 480-row gaussian forecast, and 1.52 times for a weibull AFT prediction.
    • Validated in studies/findings/crps_continuous.md, which reports all four runs. The first three found a bug in the study script, R’s qbeta() failing at tiny shape parameters, and a reference that silently missed narrow mass, each fixed before the next run.
  • Fix: quantiles no longer trust a family’s own quantile function blindly.
    • The bisection behind intervals, the pinball and interval scores, calibration widths and forecast bands took its bracket from the draws’ own quantiles.
    • Where those are wrong, as R’s qbeta() is at tiny shape parameters (off by up to 0.5 in probability), it returned a wrong quantile with no warning.
    • The bracket is now checked against the mixture’s CDF and widened until it holds. A row that cannot be bracketed is NA, with a message.
  • ilm_calibration() on a prediction is now public, as a method of illume’s generic, as ilm_scores() is. Until now it was internal.
    • It gives coverage and width by level, bias on the outcome’s scale, PIT uniformity, and for a binary outcome the calibration intercept and slope.
    • It ends with a verdict and a remedy, such as family = "nbinom" when Poisson intervals are too narrow.
    • ilm_plot_calibration() draws it.
    • Two verdicts are reworded:
      • A biased mean is now reported first. A shortfall in coverage beside it is reported as one the bias can cause, and the remedies that widen intervals wait until the mean is fixed.
      • A calibration slope whose interval lies below 0 is reported as reversed: the predictions order the outcomes the wrong way. Before, it was only called overconfident.
  • Predictions, totals, comparisons and cross-validation results keep the diagnostics they raise ($checks, or the checks attribute), and a prediction keeps the draws asked for and its seed with the generator’s kind. A forecast names its time and series columns and keeps each row’s origin: the series’ last observed time. The warnings are raised as before.
  • ilm_scores() scores a prediction by proper rules, and the scaled errors (MASE, RMSSE) take their scale either way:
    • history = train, read through the columns the prediction now records (its response, time and series);
    • naive = ilm_naive_scale(...), now exported, for a prediction with no time column, or one scale shared across models.
    The two give identical scores. When history = can’t work, the error gives the naive = call to use. The help of both says when to use each.
  • The discrete CRPS on wide supports is much faster.
    • A row wider than 2,000 values (was 10,000) is summed exactly within 50 of the outcome, and elsewhere by Euler-Maclaurin with Simpson’s rule, to an error estimate of at most 1e-6 of the score.
    • Each row records its error estimate, a flag where it’s exceeded, and the rigorous bracket width.
    • Checked against the exact sum on 105 rows, including uneven mixtures, outcomes in the far tails, steep near-Poisson rows and widths either side of 2,000: the largest relative error is 1.1e-7, and every error lies within its estimate.
    • On large counts (PBS scripts) it is 3 to 27 times faster than the block bracket it replaces.
  • A prediction whose distribution cannot be computed in some draws now stops with limn’s “draws not computed” message and the count of draws affected, in two cases that slipped through before:
    • a zero-inflated model whose zero part is not a number, where the family’s quantile function stopped with an unexplained error;
    • an ordered outcome, whose quantile is NA rather than NaN in such a draw, and which passed unflagged.
  • The discrete CRPS is faster again: 2.5 times on small counts and 1.9 times on tourism’s large counts (medians of 5 alternated runs), with the same result to rounding. The support now runs between the mixture’s own 1e-6 and 1 - 1e-6 quantiles, where the terms left out are at most 1e-12 each. Before, it was the widest of every draw’s 1e-12 quantiles. A row whose outcome falls outside that support keeps the old bounds, so it is scored exactly as before. Rows summed exactly agree with the old code to 1.2e-11 relative, and rows too wide to sum exactly now more often need no bracket.
  • ilm_average() takes weighted averages of predicted means, draw by draw, within groups of rows: standardisation over a reference population, or post-stratification with population cell sizes as weights (as in MRP). Weights are a number per row or a column name, normalised within each group, and scenarios are never averaged together. It takes a prediction of the mean. ilm_aggregate(fun = "mean") remains the verb for unweighted averages of new observations.
  • ilm_plot_fan() passes facet.args = list(free = TRUE) and ylim on to tinyplot, so each series’ panel can have its own y scale, which suits series of very different sizes. Before, the scale was fixed, and a ylim given through ... was an error. Every scale holds the history as well as the bands.
  • The CRPS of a count forecast is about 8 times faster for large counts, with the same result to rounding (2.6e-15 relative on 608 tourism forecasts; 7,232 s against 917 s, measured on a loaded machine). The mixture’s CDF comes from running sums of its mass function, and rows are grouped by support width, so a narrow row is no longer padded to the widest.
  • ilm_cv() scores a model fold by fold on data it was not fitted to: it refits the model to each fold’s training rows (illume::ilm_refit(), E6), predicts the test rows and scores them. Grouped folds predict their held-out units as new ones; other folds predict each unit as itself. Rolling folds report origin and horizon, and whether the evaluation is ex-ante or ex-post, from the covariates that vary within a series and are not named in ilm_folds(known = ). Random or blocked folds on a model with a correlation over time warn that they score interpolation. Folds can be shared out to worker processes (ncores), with the same results whatever the number. The results go straight into ilm_compare() and ilm_plot_horizon(). It needs illume 0.0.8.9001 or later for ilm_refit(), which DESCRIPTION now requires.
  • ilm_compare() gives its test as data beside the method description: a test code ("independent", "clustered", "wpe" or "dm"), the WPE test’s bandwidth m, and the DM test’s lag as used.
  • ilm_compare(by = "origin") uses the fixed-smoothing Diebold-Mariano test of Coroneo and Iacone (2020) by default (method = "wpe"): the periodogram at the first floor(T^(1/3)) Fourier frequencies of the origin means, referred to t on 2m degrees of freedom. The usual test stays as method = "dm", and warns with fewer than 100 origins over several horizons. Comparisons over several horizons now give a row pooled over them and a row for each horizon.
  • Covariate paths without building .draw blocks by hand:
    • ilm_covariate_paths() simulates a covariate’s future paths from an illume model of it. Each path is one parameter draw, the series’ latent path continued, and a new observation at each time, so the paths carry the covariate model’s own uncertainty. It returns the rows stacked into .draw blocks, ready for ilm_forecast(). Several covariates are drawn from their own models, independently.
    • ilm_as_draws() turns paths simulated elsewhere (fable’s generate(), an ensemble) into the same blocks, matching rows on by columns.
  • Covariates can be given as draws: a .draw column in newdata marks one block of rows per draw of the covariates, every block listing the same rows in the same order. Parameter draw s uses covariate draw ((s - 1) mod C) + 1, so the prediction mixes over both, and nsim is rounded up to a multiple of C, with a message.
    • Blocks that differ in their scenario, units, series or times are refused.
    • The prediction has one row per row of a block; drawn covariates show as NA where they vary, meta records C and the drawn columns, and a drawn row’s estimate is its predictive median.
    • With every parameter held, a gaussian row’s predictive distribution is the mixture over the covariate draws to 1e-8.
  • Scoring and quantiles of predictive mixtures are faster: the family is called once per block of draws rather than once per draw, which matters for small evaluations such as the quantile search. A predictive quantile of 160 rows from 1,000 draws is about 10 times faster. Results are unchanged, to 1e-12 in tests across Poisson, negative binomial, zero-inflated and gaussian-with-dispersion fits.
  • A new observation whose family overflows in some draws now stops, in the registry’s words (nan_family), instead of giving NaN quantiles and scores. It happens when a parameter sits at the edge of its range and the fit did not hold it there: a residual SD near zero, or an AR correlation near 1. The remedy named is uncertainty = "fixed" or "latent".
  • The discrete CRPS stays an exact sum up to 10^4 support values per row.
    • Beyond that, it sums each of the integrand’s two monotone pieces in blocks of d values and takes the midpoint of each block’s bracket. The error is at most d, reported per row in the scores’ crps_bound attribute.
    • On a Poisson mixture with mean 10^6 (about 1.3 x 10^5 support values, d = 13), the error was 2e-4, or 1e-7 relative, against a stated bound of 1.27.
    • The support runs between each draw’s 1e-12 and 1 - 1e-12 quantiles. The tails beyond it add at most 1e-12 times the outcome’s expected distance past its end.
  • ilm_aggregate() totals or averages a prediction over groups of its rows: a series’ forecasts over a horizon, every series at each time, or all rows.
    • Totals are taken draw by draw. A series’ path and the shared parameters and effects carry into them, and totals at different levels add up.
    • A total of new observations from a Poisson or gaussian model is an exact mixture, as in the decision “exact where the family allows”.
    • Other families’ totals are summed from four outcomes simulated per draw and held as samples. They are scored by the fair CRPS, quantiles and PITs, with no log score. The printout says which method was used.
    • An average is the total over the number of rows and is scored through it, so an average of counts keeps its whole-number steps.
    • Scenarios are never added together.
  • uncertainty = "latent" in ilm_predict() and ilm_forecast() holds every parameter at its estimate, the dispersion included, and draws only the random effects and the cells of a correlation over time, given the parameters (illume::ilm_draws(given = "parameters")). For a gaussian model with a correlation over time, that is the Kalman filter’s forecast, which treats the parameters as known, as ETS and ARIMA intervals do.
  • Every check limn makes now takes its words from one registry.
    • Each check says what was found, what it means and why the remedy helps, the remedy and how to apply it, and a reference where one exists.
    • Warnings, errors, the calibration verdicts and the help pages (the Checks section of ?ilm_predict) all compose their text from the same entries. The entries’ fields are illume’s check fields plus a reference.
    • Warnings and errors carry the filled-in fields, and a class naming the check (lmn_diagnostic, lmn_<check>), so code can catch and read them.
    • A printed prediction now notes rows that name a level the fit has not seen.
  • Forecasting: ilm_forecast(), and ilm_predict() at new times. A correlation over time (ilm_ar1(), ilm_car1() or ilm_rw1()) is carried to new times from the fit’s own parameters, with no refit.
    • A seen series continues from its fitted cells: forward past its last cell, as a bridge between two cells, and backward before its first.
    • A new series is a fresh path. AR(1) and CAR(1) paths start from their stationary distribution, and a random walk starts from zero at its first time.
    • A series’ new times are drawn as one path per draw, and rows naming the same series and time share a value. So totals over a horizon, and contrasts between scenarios, keep the path’s correlation.
    • ilm_forecast() is ilm_predict() with target = "response" and groups = "fitted".
    • For a mean or the linear predictor at a seen series’ new time, the estimate is the point forecast at the estimates: the fitted cells carried forward with no new shocks, as glmmTMB, lme4 and a Kalman filter give.
    • A forecast past the data from a model whose fixed part trends in time warns. Such a trend is assumed to carry on unchanged, so the intervals leave out any change in it (fpp3 section 10.4). The warning names a random walk, ilm_rw1(), as the stochastic trend that lets them widen. Periodic terms such as ilm_fourier() are safe to forecast and don’t count as trends. The time column comes from the correlation over time, or from ilm_future(), which now records its time and series columns.
    • as.data.frame() puts the expected value beside the estimate as mean. This is what fable reports as its point forecast, and it is what totals and squared error need. For a Poisson AR(1) series with latent SD 0.77, it was 31% to 42% above the estimate at horizons 1 to 8.
    • Each conditional step equals conditioning the process’s own covariance to 1e-12, and the paths’ draws have the joint conditional distribution of the new times given the cells.
  • ilm_predict(), the prediction engine. It gives the predictive distribution of the mean, a new observation or the linear predictor for each row of new data.
    • Parameter uncertainty is drawn jointly by illume::ilm_draws(), or with the variances held, or left out.
    • groups names how the random effects enter, and has no default for a mixed model:
      • "fitted": a unit’s own effects;
      • "new": an unseen unit’s, drawn afresh in every draw and shared by that unit’s rows;
      • "typical": effects at zero;
      • "population": the mean averaged over units, by illume’s own quadrature.
    • A level not seen in the fit is predicted as a new unit and marked.
    • A variance at the edge of its range, whose draws are not finite, stops a prediction that needs them. The message names uncertainty = "fixed" and illume’s boundary = "avoid". So does a draw that cannot be computed.
    • With fewer than about 20 levels of a random term, a prediction warns that its intervals cover below their nominal level, for means too.
      • For means and linear predictors, whatever the unit, the warning says they cover as z-intervals do.
      • For a new unit’s observation, it names reml = TRUE, which narrows the gap.
    • newdata may be a named list of scenarios, and set gives every row several values of a variable.
    • Response predictions are the same objects the scores, PITs, calibration and fan chart already use. Forecasting past a series’ observed times comes with the forecasting engine.
  • The first development version: the package skeleton, and the parts that need nothing from illume beyond what it exports today.
  • ilm_folds() builds cross-validation folds as row indices: random, grouped (whole groups held out, for predictions of new units), blocked (contiguous time, with an optional gap either side), and rolling origins (expanding or sliding windows, a horizon, a gap, and the covariates known in advance).
  • ilm_future() builds the rows a forecast needs: the next h time points after each series’ last one.
    • Columns constant within a series are copied forward.
    • Columns that vary over time are left missing and named, not guessed.
    • Time steps come from the data. For dates they are calendar units, so a month-end stays a month-end.
  • ilm_plot_fan() draws predictive distributions over time as a fan chart.
    • The median is a line, with nested central-interval bands.
    • Each series gets its own panel, with the observed history drawn first.
    • It returns the data behind the plot.
  • Diagnostic plots, each returning the data behind it:
    • ilm_plot_horizon(): each model’s mean score by forecast horizon, with standard errors clustered by origin, as in fpp3’s accuracy-by-horizon plots.
    • ilm_plot_compare(): each comparison’s difference with an interval from the same standard error as its test.
    • ilm_plot_calibration(): coverage against nominal level or, for a binary outcome, the reliability diagram with Wilson intervals, with the calibration intercept and slope beneath it.
  • ilm_pit() gives probability integral transforms. For discrete outcomes they are randomised, so they are uniform exactly when the predictive distribution is right.
  • ilm_compare() compares two or more models’ scores on the same rows, with standard errors for independent rows, clustered by a column (the HC1 cluster-robust estimator), or over rolling origins by the Diebold-Mariano test with the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold correction.
  • ilm_plot_pit() draws the PIT histogram, with a band showing where each bar falls if the predictions are right. It uses tinyplot, as illumex does.
  • Calibration of a predictive distribution (internal until illume makes ilm_calibration() a generic):
    • PIT uniformity, and coverage and width by level. Coverage is read from the PITs, so it is exactly nominal for counts too when the model is right.
    • Bias, on the outcome’s own scale.
    • For binary outcomes, the calibration intercept and slope (Van Calster et al. 2019).
    • A verdict with a remedy that exists, in illume where most are: for example family = "nbinom" when Poisson intervals are too narrow.
  • Two scaled errors join the scores:
    • mase: the absolute error over the series’ in-sample naive error.
    • rmsse: the squared error over the mean squared naive error.
    The naive error can be seasonal. Following fpp3, these make accuracy comparable across series of different scales.
  • Predictive distributions are scored from their mixture over parameter draws, with no response simulated. The scores are log, CRPS, Brier, pinball, interval, squared and absolute, and all are losses. Scoring is internal until illume makes ilm_scores() a generic, which limn will then extend.

Validation

  • A richer limn specification, registered in advance, closes most of the gap to fable’s MinT on Australian tourism (studies/findings/aggregate_mint.md). It adds a common drift and region-specific seasons (a random region-by-quarter effect) to the simple model.
    • Mean CRPS against MinT’s: 27.9 against 27.8 over the regions, 188.5 against 208.3 over the states (better), and 1,551 against 1,494 for the national total. The simple model had 45.0, 352.9 and 3,040.
    • It covered better than MinT at every level: at 80%, 0.81, 0.73 and 0.25, against 0.71, 0.45 and 0.25.
    • The simple model’s national totals were biased low. The richer model’s sit with MinT’s, both a little below the outcomes.
    • fable’s unreconciled ETS was still best at the state and national levels. One split of one dataset: a benchmark, not a test.
  • The fixed-smoothing Diebold-Mariano tests hold their size with few origins (studies/findings/compare_dm_fixed.md, R = 1000 per cell, T from 10 to 200). Over 40 null cells the 5% rejection rate of the pooled test was 0.027 to 0.119 for the usual test, 0.027 to 0.068 for WCE and 0.027 to 0.059 for WPE. At a single horizon: up to 0.126, 0.081 and 0.068. The statistics equal sandwich::lrvar() (WCE) and stats::spec.pgram() (WPE), and the critical values reproduce Coroneo and Iacone’s published ones at T = 20.
  • Covariate paths drawn by ilm_covariate_paths() from an illume model of the covariate cover as well as paths from its true process (studies/findings/covariate_draws.md, “generated” arm; R = 500 per family, on a pinned library). At 80% they covered 0.807 to 0.821 (gaussian) and 0.798 to 0.806 (Poisson). They run slightly wide at short gaussian horizons, since they also carry the covariate model’s own parameter uncertainty. With every parameter held, the paths are the covariate’s Kalman filter forecast.
    • 25 of 500 Poisson replicates failed in that arm. The covariate is noise-free, so its model’s residual SD (about 0.02 of the covariate’s SD) is not held by illume. Its joint draws reach 1e37, and a few paths overflow the Poisson forecast. The gap is illume’s to close.
  • Forecasts that mix over covariate draws cover at their nominal level, where forecasts conditional on the covariate’s point forecast do not (studies/findings/covariate_draws.md). The design is 20 series whose covariate is itself an AR(1), forecast 1 to 6 steps ahead with joint parameter draws, 500 replicates per family.
    • At 80%, drawn covariates (100 paths) covered 0.799 to 0.806 (gaussian) and 0.799 to 0.805 (Poisson), as the realised covariates did (0.806 to 0.811, 0.796 to 0.807).
    • Conditioning on the point forecast covered 0.708 falling to 0.634 (gaussian) and 0.785 to 0.767 (Poisson), worst at longer horizons, where the covariate is least known.
    • Drawn covariates’ intervals were 22% to 44% wider (gaussian) and up to 11% (Poisson), which is what the covariate’s uncertainty adds.
    • 2 of 1,000 replicates failed in every arm: a random-intercept SD at 0.02 that the fit did not hold, and a Hessian that was not positive definite.
  • The pooled Diebold-Mariano test of ilm_compare(by = "origin") (studies/findings/compare_dm_pooled.md). The design is an AR(1) series forecast 1 to H steps ahead from T origins, with 1000 replicates per cell.
    • With one horizon it holds its size: 0.038 to 0.063 at 5%.
    • With 2 or 4 horizons and 50 origins or fewer it over-rejects, at up to 0.12. By 100 or more origins it is at 0.037 to 0.069.
    • The single-horizon test at the longest horizon, which is forecast::dm.test(), over-rejects by as much, so the excess is the Diebold-Mariano test’s own with few origins, not the pooling.
    • The pooled test’s power was much higher: 0.53 against about 0.20 for either single horizon, at 200 origins with one forecaster’s noise 25% larger.
  • Totals from ilm_aggregate() cover at their nominal level (studies/findings/aggregate_coverage.md).
    • The design is 20 AR(1) series forecast 4 steps ahead, gaussian, Poisson and negative binomial, with 500 replicates per family. The variances are held, since joint draws wait on illume’s boundary holds.
    • At 90%, joint totals covered 0.888 to 0.892 for each series over the horizon, 0.891 to 0.904 across series at a step, and 0.873 to 0.905 for the grand total.
    • Summing each row’s forecast on its own under-covers where rows are correlated: 0.74 to 0.79 per series and 0.70 to 0.74 for the grand total, with intervals 22% to 34% narrower. Across series at one step it makes little difference (0.87 to 0.90).
    • When outcomes cannot be simulated (a dispersion at its limit that illume does not hold), a total now stops and names family = "poisson".
  • Against fable on Australian tourism (studies/findings/aggregate_mint.md, a benchmark, not a test), limn’s simple global model does worse, reported as found. The model is one negative binomial model with random-walk levels and a quarterly pattern common to all regions.
    • Its CRPS was 1.6 to 2 times MinT’s at every level.
    • Its national totals were biased low. They sat below the last training year while 2016-17 grew, so they covered 0 of 8 quarters at 80%. Its intervals were wider than MinT’s, so the misses are bias, not overconfidence.
    • The model has no trend, and a smoothed level lags the rise.
  • With every parameter held, forecasts are the Kalman filter’s (studies/findings/forecast_kalman.md). Gaussian AR(1), CAR(1) at irregular times, and random-walk panels, forecast 1 to 6 steps ahead with uncertainty = "latent" and compared with stats::KalmanForecast() at illume’s estimates.
    • Point forecasts agree to 9e-16.
    • With 40,000 draws, the draws’ means are within 1.5 Monte Carlo SEs, their SDs within 0.994 to 1.006 of the filter’s, and the correlation between horizons 1 and 6 within 0.008 of the filter’s.
    • Against the filter, “none” is too narrow at short horizons (0.79 to 0.92 of its SD at horizon 1), since it leaves out the last cell’s uncertainty; “fixed” and “joint” are up to 5% wider, adding the parameters’.
  • Forecast coverage by horizon, by simulation (studies/findings/forecast_coverage.md). The design is 20 series with random intercepts, observed at 8, 16 or 32 times and forecast 1 to 4 steps ahead, with 500 replicates per cell. The cells are AR(1) for gaussian and Poisson, an AR(2) fitted as AR(1), and a Poisson random walk. On the replicates where every setting ran, 90% intervals covered:
    • Plug-in: 0.850 to 0.896, under-covering everywhere.
    • With the latent’s variances held: 0.884 to 0.921.
    • With joint draws: 0.889 to 0.917, except for gaussian series of 8 times, where joint over-covers at 0.943 to 0.953. Eight times barely separate the latent from the noise, and the Gaussian approximation to their variances puts too much weight on large ones.
    • With 32 times, both settings are at 0.895 to 0.905.
    • The misspecified AR(2) cell covers 0.893 to 0.904 under joint draws.
    • Boundary fits stop joint draws until illume holds them: 36% to 40% of fits with 8 times, 13% to 19% with 16, and 0% to 4% with 32. On those replicates the held-variance intervals cover 0.85 to 0.91.
  • Forecasts have the exact conditional distribution (studies/findings/forecast_exact.md). The test data are gaussian panels of 8 series, with AR(1), CAR(1) or a random walk.
    • Latent parameters held. Forecasts at horizons 1 to 4, and values between observed times, match exact multivariate-normal conditioning at illume’s estimates within Monte Carlo error. Means are within 2.6 MC SEs, and SDs 0.992 to 1.014 times the exact ones, from 40,000 draws.
    • The reference itself. glmmTMB, with its variances mapped to the same estimates and the new rows at weight zero, reproduces it to 1.7e-15 for AR(1) and 3.9e-10 for CAR(1).
    • Joint draws. At the last observed time, limn and glmmTMB’s delta method agree, with SD ratios of 0.995 to 1.007. Ahead of it they part: at one step, limn’s spread is up to 4% wider and its centre up to 0.1 SD away, fading by four steps. limn draws each new time from its exact conditional given each draw’s parameters, while the delta method linearises in them.
  • ilm_predict() gives an independent implementation’s predictions at the same parameters (studies/findings/engine_glmmTMB.md). The comparison is glmmTMB, with every parameter held at illume’s estimates, for gaussian, Poisson and binomial random-intercept fits.
    • Known units’ means agree to 5e-12 or better, 2e-16 for a gaussian, and typical units’ exactly. A unit’s effect solved by Newton’s method in base R agrees to the same, so the remainder is the fit’s own tolerance.
    • The joint draws’ spread matches glmmTMB’s standard errors within Monte Carlo error: 0.980 to 1.012 times, for typical units (the delta method) and known units (TMB’s generalised delta method), from 5000 draws.
    • Population means equal their exact forms to 1.2e-15: exp(eta + s^2/2) for a log link, and integrate() for a logit.
    • Averaged over the sample, they reproduce illume::ilm_scenario(over = "sample"), for random intercepts and random slopes. The estimates are the same, and the interval limits agree within Monte Carlo error over 12 pairs of seeds.
  • The coverage of ilm_predict()’s intervals, by simulation (studies/findings/engine_coverage.md). The fits have random intercepts, 6 rows per group and 8 or 40 groups, across five families, with 1000 replicates per cell.
    • New observations. With joint uncertainty, central 90% intervals covered:
      • 0.891 to 0.900 with 40 groups, for seen and new units in every family;
      • 0.887 to 0.904 for seen units with 8 groups;
      • 0.872 to 0.896 for new units with 8 groups. Poisson is lowest, which is B2’s few-groups shortfall.
      Plug-in intervals covered 0.845 to 0.898, and holding the variances fell in between, so the parameters’ uncertainty is needed.
    • Means with 40 groups. 95% intervals covered 0.933 to 0.950, except a binomial seen unit’s mean at 0.914. With six 0/1 rows per unit, the Gaussian approximation to a unit’s effect is poor.
    • Means with 8 groups. Intervals under-cover as z-intervals do, which is also how illume’s confint() works. A typical unit’s 90% interval covered 0.838 to 0.861 in four families; a z-interval covers 0.856 when the truth follows t with 7 df. A binomial new unit’s mean over-covers (0.973 at 90%), because its variance is barely determined.
    • Boundary fits left out. The joint cells exclude fits whose variance sat at the boundary: 27% of binomial fits with 8 groups, and 4% or fewer elsewhere. illume is fixing the hold that makes their draws usable, and the study will be rerun then.
  • Scores match scoringRules, measured as the largest relative difference over 200 outcomes:
    • the log score to machine precision (1.4e-15 or better);
    • the CRPS to 1.2e-12 for a gaussian and 2.8e-15 for a Poisson predictive distribution;
    • for 100-draw mixtures of normals, from tight to wide, against its closed forms: the log score and the CRPS to 4.9e-12 or better.
  • The negative binomial CRPS equals the exact energy form, summed over the probability mass function, to 4.5e-14 in 45 cases (3 sizes × 3 means × 5 outcomes). That is a different computation from limn’s sum over the CDF.
    • scoringRules’ own negative binomial CRPS agrees wherever it is finite.
    • That closed form (1.1.3, through hypergeo 1.2.14) returns −Inf in 10 of the 45 cases: size 2.5 with a mean of 2 or more. So it is compared only at sizes where it is finite.
    • The negative binomial log score matches scoringRules to machine precision.
  • A clustered standard error equals sandwich::vcovCL() to 1e-12, and one over independent rows equals the paired t-test.
  • ilm_compare(by = "origin") equals forecast::dm.test() over 600 comparisons with correlated errors: to 3.6e-15 in the statistic and 3.3e-16 in the p-value. The comparisons covered 20 to 200 origins, horizons 1 to 4, and absolute and squared losses (studies/findings/compare_dm.md).
  • Rolling-origin folds are identical, row for row, to rsample::rolling_origin() in all 48 configurations tried: expanding and sliding windows, and several horizons and steps.
  • The point and interval measures agree with fabletools::accuracy() on the same forecasts (studies/findings/accuracy_fabletools.md).
    • For normal forecasts, all agree exactly: MASE and RMSSE (seasonal and not), MAE, RMSE, the 80% Winkler score, and the quantile score, which is twice limn’s pinball loss.
    • For 20-draw normal mixtures, the mean-based measures agree to 8e-16. The quantile-based ones differ by 1.5e-6, which is distributional’s root-finding tolerance: at the quantiles, the exact mixture CDF is within 3.9e-12 of its target for limn and within 4.1e-6 for distributional.
  • Grouped folds have rsample::group_vfold_cv()’s properties in all 180 random datasets: no group split, every group held out once, and group counts within one of each other (studies/findings/folds_rsample.md).
